objective: Intravenous site monitoring and maintenance within scope

brief.situation: 10:00 in a subacute rehabilitation unit. You are the LPN caring for Mrs. Grant, 86, on day 2 of IV antibiotics and maintenance fluid for pneumonia through a peripheral catheter in her left forearm. She has mild dementia and does not always report discomfort.
handover: The pump alarmed 'occlusion' twice overnight and was restarted each time.
Her 10:00 antibiotic dose is due through the same line.

Facility policy and your state's LPN IV scope here: the LPN monitors peripheral IV sites, stops an infusion and removes a peripheral catheter for infiltration, elevates the limb and reports to the RN, who assesses and arranges a new site; the LPN does not restart a line or give an IV antibiotic without the RN.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

then.log: Forearm swollen from the site to 6 cm above it, skin taut, pale and cool to touch; she winces when you press it. The other arm is normal.
Pump running at the ordered rate; no kink; the dressing is dry; the occlusion history is in the log.
Radial pulse present; fingers pink and warm; she moves them.
She says it is 'tight' and grimaces when the arm is moved.

why.question: What is happening at Mrs. Grant's IV site, and what do you do within your role?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Infiltration: IV fluid leaking into the tissue around the vein, shown by swelling, taut, cool and pale skin and pain above the site; the occlusion alarms were a clue.
parts.modelAnswer: The IV has infiltrated: the fluid is going into her forearm instead of the vein. That's why it's swollen, tight, cool and pale and hurts, and why the pump kept alarming.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Stops the infusion, removes the catheter per policy, elevates the arm, checks circulation, reports to the RN for a new site and the antibiotic, documents and marks the swelling; does not flush or restart.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop it, take the catheter out per policy, raise her arm, check her hand, and tell the RN so she can start a new line for the antibiotic. Document it and mark the edge. No flushing and no restarting.

noProgress.rationale: An infiltrating IV left running and unreported an hour on is harm here.

safe.body: You recognized infiltration, stopped and removed it, elevated the arm, checked circulation and reported to the RN within minutes. That is the expert path.

scoring.modelReasoning: Infiltration is IV fluid or medication leaking into the tissue around the vein; the site swells, the skin turns taut, cool and pale, and it hurts. Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and place a new one at a different site, elevate the limb, notify, and use compresses as directed. Within this LPN's scope: stop, remove per policy, elevate, check circulation, report to the RN, who restarts the line and gives the antibiotic, and document. Never flush through an infiltrated site or restart the pump.
